input.title: Informal Scholarly Circles and the Origins of the Royal Society of London

prompt.scenario: In the period c. 1450 to c. 1750, European scholars increasingly studied the natural world through observation, experiment and shared discussion. In seventeenth-century England, an informal circle of such scholars became the core of the Royal Society of London, which received its formal organization in the early 1660s.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Briefly describe ONE feature of how the group of scholars in the excerpt organized its activities before the Royal Society's formal organization in 1662.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE intellectual or technological development in Europe from c. 1600 to c. 1700, other than those named in the excerpt, that helps explain why scholars like those in the excerpt formed groups to investigate the natural world.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE similarity or difference between the organization of scientific or astronomical study described in the excerpt and the organization of such study in ONE state outside Western Europe from c. 1450 to c. 1750.

requirements: Each part asks for ONE answer worth 1 point.
Part A must draw on what the excerpt itself says.
Part B must use a specific development from c. 1600 to c. 1700 that is not named in the excerpt.
Part C must name a specific state outside Western Europe and make an explicit comparison with the excerpt.

rows.task_specific: Describe one feature of the group's organization drawn from the excerpt: regular weekly meetings; meetings held at a private home, a tavern and Gresham College rather than one official building; members from many fields (mathematics, astronomy, medicine, physiology, political economy, invention); a member from abroad (Haak from the Pfalz); a practical, experimental focus (Goddard carrying out experiments, interest in navigation and boats); the group existing informally from about 1645, long before the formal organization of 1662.

descriptors.0: The response does not describe a feature supported by the excerpt, or only restates the title or the date with no description.
descriptors.1: The response accurately describes one feature of how the group met or was made up, as shown in the excerpt.

rows.task_specific: Explain one specific development from c. 1600 to c. 1700, not named in the excerpt, that helps account for collaborative inquiry, with a clear link to group study. Examples: Francis Bacon's call for organized, collective empirical research; growth of print and letter-writing networks such as Marin Mersenne's correspondence; new instruments like the telescope and microscope; the challenge to inherited authority from heliocentric astronomy argued by Galileo; Descartes's method.

descriptors.0: The response names a development that is not specific, falls outside the period, is only from the excerpt, or does not explain the link to group inquiry.
descriptors.1: The response explains one accurate, specific development from the stated years and how it encouraged scholars to work together.

rows.task_specific: Name a specific state outside Western Europe and explain one similarity or difference with the excerpt's informal, voluntary circle. Examples: the Ottoman observatory at Istanbul under Taqi al-Din, founded and then pulled down by the state in the late 1570s and 1580; the Qing Directorate of Astronomy employing Jesuits such as Ferdinand Verbiest under the Kangxi Emperor; the observatories built by Jai Singh II in Mughal-era India in the early eighteenth century; Russian state-sponsored learning under Peter the Great, including the Academy of Sciences planned in 1724.

descriptors.0: The response does not name a valid state outside Western Europe, gets the facts wrong, or describes the other case without comparing it to the excerpt.
descriptors.1: The response explains one accurate similarity or difference between the excerpt's group and the organization of study in a named state outside Western Europe.

scoring_notes: ALTON reference — not official AP scoring
Each part is scored separately and earns 0 or 1 point; one correct answer is enough even if a second idea is weak, unless the response contradicts itself.
In Part B, responses that name Harvey, Hobbes, Hartlib, Boyle or Gresham College alone do not earn the point, because those are named in the excerpt.
Do not reward a claim that the Royal Society was the first scientific society anywhere; earlier bodies such as the Accademia dei Lincei in Rome existed.
In Part C, a general statement such as 'other places also did science' with no named state and no comparison does not earn the point.

a: The scholars met on a regular weekly schedule, according to the excerpt, which made their discussions a steady habit rather than a single event.
The group had no single official home and met in a private house in Wood Street, at the Bull's Head Tavern in Cheapside and at Gresham College.
The circle brought together men from many fields, including mathematics, astronomy, medicine and political economy, and even a scholar from the Pfalz in the German lands.

The group worked informally for years, from about 1645, before it gained a definite organization as the Royal Society in 1662, and it valued hands-on experiment, as shown by Goddard always being willing to carry one out.
b: Francis Bacon's writings in the 1620s, including New Atlantis with its imagined research house, argued that knowledge of nature should come from organized, shared observation and experiment, and English natural philosophers took up that program.

Printing and the growth of letter networks, such as the correspondence that Marin Mersenne kept up in Paris during the 1630s and 1640s, let scholars exchange results across borders and encouraged them to meet and compare findings.
New instruments such as the telescope and the microscope produced observations that one person could not easily confirm alone, so scholars gathered to watch, repeat and check experiments.

Galileo's telescopic observations and his defense of heliocentrism undermined inherited authorities like Aristotle and Ptolemy, which pushed scholars to test claims through experiment and discussion with one another.
c: Different: the Ottoman observatory at Istanbul, led by Taqi al-Din in the 1570s, was founded with the sultan's backing and then pulled down by state order in 1580, while the London circle began as a voluntary group meeting in houses and taverns.

Different: in Qing China, astronomy was a state office, and the Kangxi Emperor employed Jesuits such as Ferdinand Verbiest in the Directorate of Astronomy to fix the calendar, unlike the private, self-organized London group.
Similar: like the London circle, which brought in Theodore Haak from the German lands, the Qing Directorate of Astronomy drew on foreign expertise by employing European Jesuit astronomers.

Different: in early eighteenth-century India, the ruler Jai Singh II built large stone observatories such as the one at Jaipur under his own patronage, whereas the London scholars started without a royal patron and only later received a charter.

facts: The Royal Society of London was founded in 1660 and received a royal charter from Charles II in 1662.
The Royal Society began publishing Philosophical Transactions in 1665, with Henry Oldenburg as editor.
Earlier scientific academies existed in Europe, including the Accademia dei Lincei in Rome, founded in 1603.
The French Academie des Sciences was founded in 1666 with royal support under Louis XIV and his minister Colbert.
Francis Bacon's New Atlantis, published in 1626, described an imagined research institution called Salomon's House.
Robert Boyle, working with Robert Hooke, used an air pump in experiments on air and vacuum.
Isaac Newton's Principia was published in 1687 with the approval of the Royal Society.
common_pitfalls: Claiming the Royal Society was the first scientific organization in the world.
In Part B, reusing people or places named in the excerpt, such as Harvey or Gresham College, instead of a new development.
In Part C, describing a non-European example without making an explicit comparison to the excerpt.
Using examples from after 1750, such as nineteenth-century institutions.
Treating Libby's 1917 praise of the members' humility and good will as established fact rather than as the author's characterization.
contextualization_ideas: The Scientific Revolution's shift toward empirical observation and mathematical description of nature.
The English Civil Wars and Interregnum of the 1640s and 1650s, the years when the informal group was meeting, and the Restoration of Charles II in 1660.
outside_evidence: Accademia dei Lincei (1603)
Academie des Sciences (1666)
Philosophical Transactions (1665)
Marin Mersenne's correspondence network
Francis Bacon's New Atlantis
Taqi al-Din's Istanbul observatory
Ferdinand Verbiest and the Qing Directorate of Astronomy
Jai Singh II's observatories
reasoning_types: Sourcing and reading a secondary source

doc_uses.usable_for: Evidence of the informal, many-disciplined, regular meetings that came before the Royal Society's formal organization in 1662
doc_uses.sourcing: A 1917 American textbook on the history of science; its admiring tone toward the members reflects the author's interpretation, written long after the events.

input.title: Changing Understandings of Human Activity and the Natural Environment, c. 1860 to c. 2000

prompt.scenario: From the middle of the nineteenth century onward, writers, scientists, and governments in many parts of the world described how farming, logging, grazing, industry, and large state projects were changing land, water, and air. The seven documents include a scholar's warning from the 1860s, a naturalist's account of forest reserves, a chemist's calculations about carbon dioxide and temperature, a photograph from the 1930s, a table of atmospheric measurements, and two reference studies from the 1990s.
prompt.task: Evaluate the extent to which understandings of the relationship between human activity and the natural environment changed from c. 1860 to c. 2000.
requirements: Respond to the prompt with a historically defensible thesis or claim that establishes a line of reasoning.
Describe a broader historical context relevant to the prompt.
Support an argument in response to the prompt using at least four documents.
Use at least one additional piece of specific historical evidence (beyond that found in the documents) relevant to an argument about the prompt.
For at least two documents, explain how or why the document's point of view, purpose, historical situation, and/or audience is relevant to an argument.
Use evidence to corroborate, qualify, or modify an argument that addresses the prompt.

rows.task_specific: A claim that evaluates how far understandings changed between c. 1860 and c. 2000, for example by weighing continuity in concern about resource exploitation against change in scale (local land to global atmosphere), in method (moral warning to measurement), or in who responded (individuals to states and international bodies).

descriptors.0: The response restates the prompt, offers no evaluative claim about extent of change, or places the claim outside the introduction or conclusion.
descriptors.1: The response makes a defensible claim about the extent of change that sets up a line of reasoning, such as change in scale alongside continuity in concern about exploitation.

rows.task_specific: Describes developments relevant to the prompt, such as industrialization and rising coal use, the spread of commercial agriculture and settlement onto grasslands and forests, Cold War-era state development projects, or post-1970 global environmental diplomacy, and connects them to the argument.

descriptors.0: The response gives no relevant context or only a passing phrase.
descriptors.1: The response describes a broader historical development before, during, or continuing after the period and links it to the argument.

rows.task_specific: Accurately uses the content of documents; the higher point requires using at least four documents to support an argument about change or continuity in understandings of human-environment relations.

descriptors.0: The response does not accurately describe the content of at least three documents.
descriptors.1: The response accurately describes the content of at least three documents in relation to the topic, or supports an argument with fewer than four.
descriptors.2: The response uses the content of at least four documents to support an argument that answers the prompt.

rows.task_specific: One specific piece of evidence not in the documents, explained in relation to the argument, such as Rachel Carson's Silent Spring (1962), the 1972 Stockholm UN conference, the Montreal Protocol (1987), the creation of the IPCC (1988), or the Kyoto Protocol (1997).

descriptors.0: The response offers no outside evidence or only names something without connecting it to the argument.
descriptors.1: The response describes a specific piece of outside evidence and explains how it supports or qualifies the argument.

rows.task_specific: For two documents, explains how point of view, purpose, historical situation, or audience shapes the document's use, for example the government sponsorship of the 1936 photograph or the U.S. government origin of the 1991 Soviet study at the end of the Cold War.

descriptors.0: The response does not explain sourcing for at least two documents, or only labels the author without explanation.
descriptors.1: The response explains how or why the sourcing of at least two documents matters to an argument.

rows.task_specific: Shows a complex grasp, for example by explaining both continuity and change, by tracing how state and international responses grew while results stayed limited, or by corroborating across scientific, visual, and governmental evidence and sourcing most documents.

descriptors.0: The response does not show a complex understanding, or does so only in a single sentence.
descriptors.1: The response develops nuanced reasoning throughout the argument, such as weighing continuity against change or explaining multiple causes of shifting understanding.

scoring_notes: ALTON reference — not official AP scoring
The prompt period runs to c. 2000; Document 5's 2010 and 2020 values may be used as a continuation of the trend but are not required.

Document 3's excerpt states a physical relationship between carbon dioxide and temperature; it does not itself mention human emissions. Do not reward claims that the excerpt blames fuel burning, though students may use outside knowledge carefully.
Do not credit sourcing that claims an author personally saw the events or places described unless the document says so.
Credit arguments of strong change, strong continuity, or mixed positions equally if well supported.

defensible_theses: Understandings changed significantly in scale: mid-nineteenth-century observers like Marsh and Muir focused on visible damage to forests and land, while twentieth-century science and measurement, shown by Arrhenius and the Mauna Loa data, extended concern to the global atmosphere, and by the 1990s environmental problems had become matters for international conferences.

Understandings changed only to a limited extent: from Marsh in 1864 to the Soviet and Brazilian studies of the 1990s, observers kept describing the same basic pattern of economic exploitation (logging, grazing, plowing, irrigation, energy production) degrading land and water, even as the tools for measuring that damage improved.

The largest change was in who took responsibility: individual writers warned of damage in the nineteenth century, but by the twentieth century governments documented, measured, and sometimes tried to manage environmental harm, although documents from the 1990s show that state attention was often limited or uneven.
contextualization_ideas: Industrialization from the late eighteenth century greatly expanded coal and later oil use, and the spread of settler farming and ranching onto grasslands and forests in the Americas and elsewhere transformed landscapes, which set the stage for warnings like those of Marsh and Muir.

In the twentieth century, states pursued rapid agricultural and industrial development, including Soviet planned economies and developmental states in Latin America, often treating nature as a resource to be mastered for growth.

After the 1960s an environmental movement and international diplomacy grew, including the 1972 Stockholm UN Conference on the Human Environment, the 1987 Montreal Protocol, and the 1992 Rio conference, making the environment a global political issue.
outside_evidence: Rachel Carson's Silent Spring (1962) warned about the effects of pesticides such as DDT and helped spark the modern environmental movement.
The first Earth Day was held in 1970.
The 1972 UN Conference on the Human Environment in Stockholm was the first major UN conference focused on the environment.
The Montreal Protocol (1987) phased out chemicals that deplete the ozone layer.
The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change was created in 1988, and the Kyoto Protocol of 1997 set emissions targets for industrialized nations.
Yellowstone became the first U.S. national park in 1872, and John Muir co-founded the Sierra Club in 1892.
The Dust Bowl resulted from severe drought combined with the plowing of Great Plains grasslands; the U.S. created the Soil Conservation Service in 1935.
The Bhopal gas leak in India in 1984 killed thousands of people and became a symbol of industrial hazards in developing countries.
Brazilian rubber tapper and forest activist Chico Mendes was murdered in 1988, drawing international attention to Amazon deforestation.
Wangari Maathai founded the Green Belt Movement in Kenya in 1977 to promote tree planting.

doc_uses.usable_for: Early evidence that human action was seen as capable of degrading the whole earth, including its soils, surface, and climate, framed in moral terms of crime and improvidence.
doc_uses.sourcing: Marsh was a U.S. diplomat whose posts in the Ottoman Empire and Italy gave him a career outside the United States; his warning about the earth as a whole, published in 1864, shows that concern about human-caused damage was not confined to one country or to the twentieth century.

doc_uses.usable_for: Shows concern about logging, fire, and grazing on forest reserves and the idea that land should be protected; supports continuity in worry about resource exploitation.
doc_uses.sourcing: Muir was a naturalist writing a book about national parks in 1901; his purpose of defending the reserves helps explain his vivid language, such as calling sheep hoofed locusts, and his hostility toward lumbermen and shepherds.

doc_uses.usable_for: Shows a shift toward quantitative, physical understanding of how small changes in atmospheric carbon dioxide affect global temperature.
doc_uses.sourcing: Arrhenius was a chemist writing a book on the evolution of the universe; the scientific setting explains why the excerpt is about physical calculation rather than human blame, which limits its use as evidence of concern about human emissions.

doc_uses.usable_for: Visual evidence of soil erosion and dust storms on the Great Plains in the 1930s, a disaster linked to farming practices and drought.
doc_uses.sourcing: The photograph was made for the Resettlement Administration, a U.S. government agency, so its dramatic framing of the dust cloud may reflect the government's interest in showing how serious rural conditions were; it also shows the state itself recording environmental harm.

doc_uses.usable_for: Shows a steady rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide from about 317 in 1960 to about 370 in 2000 and 414 in 2020, evidence of measurable global change.
doc_uses.sourcing: The data come from a U.S. government science agency and earlier Scripps measurements; long-term instrument records reflect a new, systematic way of tracking environmental change, though the table alone does not state causes.

doc_uses.usable_for: Shows that large state projects, Chernobyl and the diversion of Aral Sea rivers for cotton irrigation, produced major environmental disasters; supports the idea that development priorities caused harm.
doc_uses.sourcing: Written for the U.S. government in 1991, as the Cold War ended and before the Soviet collapse, the study may emphasize Soviet neglect partly because of its rivalry-era perspective, though the disasters it names are well documented.

doc_uses.usable_for: Shows Amazon deforestation and pollution becoming international issues, the 1992 Rio UN conference, and the language of sustainable development, while noting that Brazilian government attention waned.
doc_uses.sourcing: As a U.S. government reference work describing another country, it offers an outside observer's view of Brazil's policies; its note that attention waned after Eco-92 shows the authors assessing gaps between international concern and national action.

evidence_map.line: Understanding shifted from local or regional damage to land and forests toward a global, atmospheric view of human impact.
Continuity: observers across the whole period saw economic exploitation of land and water (logging, grazing, plowing, irrigation, energy) as degrading the environment.
Governments and international institutions increasingly documented, measured, and addressed environmental harm.
Understanding became more scientific and quantitative, moving from moral warning to measurement.

common_pitfalls: Describing each document in sequence without making an argument about the extent of change.
Claiming that Document 3 blames human fuel burning for warming; the excerpt only describes a physical relationship.
Treating Document 5 as proof of causes rather than as a record of rising concentrations.
Saying Marsh, Muir, or the reference-study authors personally witnessed the events described.
Focusing only on the United States and ignoring the Soviet, Brazilian, and international evidence.
Describing the Dust Bowl only as a natural drought without noting the role of farming practices.
Sourcing by simply naming the author or date without explaining why it matters.
facts: George Perkins Marsh published Man and Nature in 1864.
John Muir published Our National Parks in 1901 and co-founded the Sierra Club in 1892.
Svante Arrhenius was a Swedish chemist who calculated the effect of carbon dioxide on the earth's temperature.
Arthur Rothstein photographed the Texas Panhandle for the Resettlement Administration in March 1936.
The Mauna Loa carbon dioxide record began in 1958 under C. David Keeling.
The Chernobyl nuclear accident occurred in 1986 in Soviet Ukraine.
Rivers feeding the Aral Sea were diverted for irrigation, especially for cotton, causing the sea to shrink dramatically.
The UN Conference on Environment and Development was held in Rio de Janeiro in June 1992.

input.title: LEQ: Continuity and Change in Responses to Famine, Disease, and Environmental Stress, c. 1200 to c. 1750

prompt.scenario: Between c. 1200 and c. 1750, societies across Afro-Eurasia and the Americas faced harvest failures, epidemic disease, floods, droughts, and the cooling of the Little Ice Age. Rulers, religious institutions, and local communities answered these crises with granaries, labor laws, public works, quarantines, charity, new crops, and new medical practices, and sometimes with persecution or coercion.
prompt.task: Evaluate the extent to which state and community responses to famine, disease, and environmental stress changed from c. 1200 to c. 1750. You are not expected to address the entire time period.
requirements: Respond to the prompt with a historically defensible thesis or claim that establishes a line of reasoning.
Describe a broader historical context relevant to the prompt.
Support an argument in response to the prompt using at least two pieces of specific and relevant evidence.
Use historical reasoning (continuity and change) to frame or structure an argument that addresses the prompt.
Use evidence to demonstrate a complex understanding of the historical development that is the focus of the prompt.

rows.task_specific: A claim that judges how far responses to famine, disease, or environmental stress changed between c. 1200 and c. 1750, and gives a line of reasoning such as continued reliance on stored grain and religious ritual alongside new quarantine practices, new crops, or colonial labor policies.

descriptors.0: Gives no defensible claim, simply restates the prompt, or makes a claim that does not address the extent of change or continuity in responses.
descriptors.1: Makes a defensible claim about the extent of change or continuity in responses to famine, disease, or environmental stress and indicates the reasons or categories that will organize the argument.

rows.task_specific: Describes a broader setting such as the Mongol-era networks that spread the plague in the 1300s, the cooling and climate instability of the Little Ice Age, the Columbian Exchange after 1492, or the growth of bureaucratic and gunpowder empires that could collect and redistribute resources.

descriptors.0: Offers no relevant context or only a passing phrase not tied to the argument.
descriptors.1: Describes a broader development before, during, or around the period and links it to how states or communities responded to crisis.

rows.task_specific: Specific examples of responses, such as the English Ordinance of Labourers of 1349, the 30-day isolation rule at Ragusa in 1377, Inca storehouses supplied through mit'a labor in the Andes, Chinese ever-normal granaries, Tokugawa promotion of sweet potatoes after the Kyoho famine, or Spanish resettlement of Indigenous communities in central Mexico and the Andes after epidemics.

descriptors.0: Provides no specific examples, or only vague references to disease or famine.
descriptors.1: Identifies at least two specific, accurate examples relevant to responses to famine, disease, or environmental stress.
descriptors.2: Uses at least two specific, accurate examples to support an argument about the extent of change or continuity in responses.

rows.task_specific: Uses continuity and change to frame the argument, for example by contrasting responses from before and after 1450 or before and after the Columbian Exchange; a complex answer might weigh change against continuity, compare regions, explain why some responses changed while others persisted, or tie state relief to labor control and political legitimacy.

descriptors.0: Lists examples without historical reasoning about change or continuity.
descriptors.1: Uses continuity and change to frame or structure an argument about state and community responses.
descriptors.2: Shows a complex understanding, for example by explaining both change and continuity, by analyzing several causes of change, or by making a supported cross-regional comparison or connection.

scoring_notes: ALTON reference — not official AP scoring

Examples may come from any region; an essay need not include the Americas, but American examples must name the specific region and its own labor system, such as the Andean mit'a, the Spanish colonial mita at Potosi, or the encomienda in New Spain.
Persecution, scapegoating, and coercive labor policies count as responses and can support the argument; graders should credit accurate analysis of them without requiring moral judgment.
Claims that one crisis by itself caused the fall of a dynasty or empire should not earn credit as evidence unless the essay qualifies them; coincidence of crisis and rebellion may be described.
The thesis may appear in the introduction or conclusion but must be in one place, not pieced together from scattered sentences.

defensible_theses: Responses changed significantly in method after c. 1450 as states adopted quarantine, new American crops, and in some places variolation, but the underlying aims of feeding subjects to preserve order and blaming or controlling vulnerable groups continued from the Black Death era.

Continuity outweighed change: from the Song-Yuan-Ming granary tradition to Inca storehouses to Tokugawa relief, states relied mostly on stored food, labor mobilization, and religious ritual, while truly new practices such as lazarettos and the spread of sweet potatoes added to these tools rather than replacing them.

Responses changed most in the Americas, where Spanish colonizers answered epidemic population collapse with resettlement and coercive labor drafts that replaced Andean and Mesoamerican systems of reciprocal redistribution, while Afro-Eurasian states mostly expanded older relief practices.
contextualization_ideas: Mongol-era trade and military networks across Eurasia in the 1200s and 1300s helped carry the plague that became the Black Death in the 1340s, shaping the first great wave of responses.
Climate cooling and instability associated with the Little Ice Age brought harvest failures in many regions during the 1600s, a time often called the seventeenth-century crisis.

The Columbian Exchange after 1492 spread Afro-Eurasian diseases to the Americas and American crops such as maize, potatoes, and sweet potatoes to Afro-Eurasia, changing both the crises and the tools for answering them.
outside_evidence: England's Ordinance of Labourers (1349) and Statute of Labourers (1351) tried to fix wages at pre-plague levels after the Black Death caused labor shortages.
Ragusa (Dubrovnik) required a 30-day isolation of arrivals in 1377, and Venice set up a permanent lazaretto in 1423, early institutional quarantine measures.

During the Black Death, Jewish communities in many European towns, including Strasbourg in 1349, were attacked after false accusations of causing the plague, while flagellant movements staged public penance.
The Great Famine of 1315 to 1317 in northern Europe brought widespread starvation after repeated harvest failures.
Chinese dynasties maintained ever-normal granaries to buy grain in good years and sell or distribute it in bad years; the Qing expanded this granary system in the 1700s.
Sweet potatoes and maize from the Americas spread in China during the 1600s and 1700s and helped farmers cultivate hilly land and support population growth.
In the Andes, the Inca state used mit'a rotational labor to build roads and terraces and to fill qollqa storehouses that held food for times of shortage.

After smallpox struck Tenochtitlan in 1520 and later epidemics reduced Indigenous populations in central Mexico, Spanish authorities consolidated surviving communities into congregaciones, or reducciones, for labor, tribute, and conversion.
In the 1570s Viceroy Francisco de Toledo reorganized the mita in the Andes into a colonial labor draft that sent Indigenous workers to the Potosi silver mines.
The Spanish Crown's New Laws of 1542 sought to limit encomienda abuses amid the decline of Indigenous populations.
Tokugawa Yoshimune's government promoted sweet potato cultivation, associated with the scholar Aoki Kon'yo, after the Kyoho famine of 1732 to 1733.
The Mamluk sultan Qalawun founded a large hospital in Cairo in the 1280s, an example of charitable medical institutions in the Islamic world, often supported through waqf endowments.
Variolation, deliberate exposure to smallpox material, was practiced in China and the Ottoman Empire; Lady Mary Wortley Montagu observed it in Istanbul and promoted it in England around 1721.
England's Poor Law of 1601 made parishes responsible for relief of the poor through local taxes.
reasoning_types: Causation (why some responses shifted, such as new crops after the Columbian Exchange)
Comparison across regions as a complexity move
common_pitfalls: Describing the crises themselves (plague deaths, famine) without discussing how states or communities responded.
Treating the Black Death or the Little Ice Age as the single cause of a dynasty's fall rather than one factor among several.
Writing only about Europe, or only listing examples without a judgment on the extent of change.
Using vague phrases like 'Native Americans were forced to work' instead of naming the region and labor system, such as the Andean mit'a or the Potosi mita.
Confusing the pre-colonial Inca mit'a, built on reciprocity and state redistribution, with the colonial Spanish mita at Potosi.
Moving well past 1750 to examples such as Jenner's vaccine of 1796 without tying them back to the period.
facts: The Black Death spread through Afro-Eurasia from the 1340s, reaching Europe and the Mediterranean in 1347 to 1351.
England issued the Ordinance of Labourers in 1349 and the Statute of Labourers in 1351.
Ragusa adopted a 30-day isolation rule in 1377; the word quarantine comes from the later 40-day period.
Smallpox struck Tenochtitlan in 1520.
The New Laws were issued in 1542.
Francisco de Toledo was viceroy of Peru in the 1570s and organized the Potosi mita.
The Kyoho famine occurred in 1732 to 1733 under Tokugawa Yoshimune.
England's Poor Law was enacted in 1601.
